content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building executive summaries — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary executive summaries tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. When executive summaries guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
2. Keep executive summaries changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
3. When multiple executive summaries strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
4. When executive summaries decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
5. Measure before optimizing any executive summaries bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
6. Validate executive summaries outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
7. Surface known limitations of a chosen executive summaries approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
8. Document any non-obvious executive summaries decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
9. State assumptions about executive summaries explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
10. Before starting executive summaries work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not silently drop executive summaries edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of executive summaries correctness.
- Avoid introducing new executive summaries abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not apply generic executive summaries advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid mixing unrelated executive summaries concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about executive summaries over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
